article.headline: A Supply-Chain Map for Trading Short AGI Timelines
article.lede: The interesting investment question for believers in short AGI timelines isn't which software model wins but which physical chokepoints all AI computation depends on. @_Lonis_, a retail investor, spent a weekend mapping the AI hardware stack fifteen layers deep — from lithium mines and rare-earth deposits through silicon wafers and advanced packaging substrates — color-coding each company by how much of its revenue already flows from AI demand. The chart is personal reference, not investment advice, but its analytical framework is the same one institutional analysts use: who is indispensable, and has the market noticed yet?
article.body:
The premise rests on a bet about *AGI timelines* — shorthand for predictions of when AI systems will achieve general human-level capability across essentially any cognitive task. If that threshold arrives within years rather than decades, the argument goes, capital advantages flow not to whoever picks the right *foundation model* but to whoever controls the physical infrastructure that all AI training and inference must pass through. The chart identifies, at each rung of that stack, which companies cannot easily be routed around.

The outermost layer is raw materials: **platinum-group metals** (*PGMs*), rare earths, lithium, copper, and nickel — feedstocks for magnets, battery chemistry, and conductors used throughout the chain. Companies flagged include Sibanye-Stillwater (SBSW), the South African miner with roughly a fifth of global PGM output; MP Materials (MP), operator of the only large-scale US rare-earth mine at Mountain Pass, California; Albemarle (ALB), one of the world's largest lithium chemicals producers; Freeport-McMoRan (FCX), the largest publicly traded copper miner; and Sumitomo Metal Mining (5713.T) for nickel. Estimated AI revenue exposure for all five sits in the single digits — these are broad commodity businesses whose prices are set by global demand across many industries, not by GPU build-outs alone.

One layer up, the picture concentrates. **Silicon wafers** — the purified discs on which chip circuitry is etched — are produced by a tight oligopoly: Shin-Etsu Chemical (4063.T), a Japanese conglomerate estimated to hold roughly a third of global *300mm wafer* capacity; SUMCO (3436.T), its domestic rival at around a quarter; and Germany's Siltronic (WAF.DE) at roughly 12%. More striking is the *ABF substrate* segment. *Ajinomoto Build-up Film* (ABF) is a laminate layer critical to advanced chip packaging — it connects a processor die to its circuit board at densities older materials cannot match. Ibiden (4062.T) and Unimicron (3037.TW) together command a dominant share of this market, and the chart estimates their AI revenue exposure at 30–40%, making these among the earliest genuinely AI-heavy names in the upstream portion of the stack.

The visualization encodes two variables simultaneously: box width represents a company's market share within its layer, and color encodes the share of revenue attributed to AI demand, breaking at under-15%, 15–30%, and above 30%. A wide, deeply saturated box signals a bottleneck that already knows it is one — potential pricing power in both directions. The creator is evidently most interested in the upper two color bands, where AI demand is material but perhaps not yet so visible that equity markets have priced it fully.

The OCR captures only the first three of fifteen layers; the remaining twelve presumably pass through lithography and fab equipment — where ASML (ASML) holds a near-monopoly on *extreme ultraviolet (EUV)* lithography machines, the tools that print the finest circuit features on leading-edge chips — then through chip fabrication, memory, advanced packaging, and data-center infrastructure. Those deeper layers contain the AI names most widely followed by equity markets. The upstream focus here reflects a contrarian logic: the closer a company sits to the earth, the less likely analysts have already assigned it an AI premium.

concepts.definition: Predictions — ranging from a few years to many decades — about when artificial general intelligence will arrive. AGI refers to AI systems capable of matching or exceeding human cognitive performance across essentially any task, not just the narrow domains where today's models excel. Timeline beliefs drive significant investment, research, and strategic decisions across the technology industry.

A large AI model trained on broad data at scale and then adapted for many specific tasks — examples include the GPT family, Claude, and Gemini. The term highlights that these models function as a base layer on which many downstream applications are built, analogous to an operating system underlying software.

Six chemically related metallic elements — platinum, palladium, rhodium, ruthenium, iridium, and osmium — found together in ore deposits and mined primarily in South Africa and Russia. They are used in catalytic converters, industrial catalysts, and electronic components. PGM prices are notoriously volatile, driven by automotive and industrial demand.

A thin, flat disc of highly purified silicon crystal — typically 300mm in diameter for advanced manufacturing — on which transistors and circuit components are fabricated. Wafer quality and diameter constrain what circuit geometries are achievable; a small handful of companies produce essentially all of the world's advanced supply.

The dominant size standard for leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing, where 300mm (roughly 12-inch) silicon discs yield more chips per wafer than older 200mm substrates, reducing per-chip cost. Converting a fabrication plant to 300mm requires billions in capital investment, creating high barriers to entry and concentrating supply among few producers.

Ajinomoto Build-up Film (ABF) substrate is an advanced organic packaging layer that electrically connects a processor die to its circuit board, enabling higher interconnect density and signal integrity than older ceramic or basic organic packages allow. It was first developed by food company Ajinomoto as a byproduct of amino-acid research and is now critical to high-performance chip packaging. Supply is highly concentrated in Japan and Taiwan.

Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography uses 13.5-nanometer wavelength light to print chip features far smaller than older deep-ultraviolet processes allow, enabling the most advanced semiconductor nodes (currently 3nm and below). ASML is the only company in the world that manufactures EUV machines, giving it a structural monopoly on the equipment needed for leading-edge chip production.

article.fact_check: The market-share and AI-revenue figures in the visualization are the creator's own estimates; no primary sources or methodology are cited, so all percentages should be treated as informed approximations rather than audited data. The OCR label 'Sumitomo Metal' in the raw-materials layer is ambiguous: the former Sumitomo Metal Industries merged into Nippon Steel in 2012 and is no longer an independent entity; the nickel-producing company is Sumitomo Metal Mining (5713.T), a separately listed firm, which is almost certainly what the visualization intends. The broad structural claims — ASML's EUV dominance, Shin-Etsu's wafer leadership — are consistent with publicly available industry data.

ticker_mp.name: MP Materials Corp.
ticker_mp.blurb: MP Materials operates Mountain Pass in California, the only producing rare-earth mining and processing facility in the United States. The company extracts and refines neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide and in 2025 opened a full-scale permanent magnet manufacturing plant in Fort Worth, Texas. Its customers include General Motors under a long-term supply agreement for electric-vehicle traction motor magnets, and the U.S. government has backed the company with roughly $400 million in strategic investment.
ticker_mp.recent: In early 2025 MP Materials inaugurated its Fort Worth magnet facility and began commercial NdFeB magnet shipments to GM, a landmark for domestic rare-earth supply-chain independence. The company's AI revenue exposure remains indirect — data-center cooling fans and robotics actuators use its magnets — but the robotics angle is drawing increasing investor attention as humanoid robot programs scale.

sources.title: 2025 to be a Defining Year for the Rare Earth Magnet Market — IDTechEx

ticker_alb.name: Albemarle Corporation
ticker_alb.blurb: Albemarle is one of the world's largest producers of lithium compounds, supplying battery-grade lithium hydroxide and carbonate to electric-vehicle and energy-storage markets. It also produces bromine and specialty chemicals. The company holds roughly 16% of global lithium market share and operates mines in Chile, Australia, and the United States. Its AI revenue exposure is indirect — lithium's primary demand driver remains EV batteries — but data-center battery backup systems and robotics batteries create a secondary link.
ticker_alb.recent: Albemarle has faced significant margin pressure through 2025 and into 2026 as lithium spot prices remained well below 2022 peaks amid a supply glut and slower-than-expected EV adoption in key markets. The company has responded by curtailing production and deferring expansion projects. AI-related demand for lithium is real but remains a small fraction of total consumption.

sources.title: Neodymium Market Size & Share | Grand View Research

ticker_fcx.name: Freeport-McMoRan Inc.
ticker_fcx.blurb: Freeport-McMoRan is the world's largest publicly traded copper producer, operating the Grasberg mine in Indonesia — one of the largest copper and gold deposits on Earth — alongside mines in North and South America. Copper is a critical input for data-center power infrastructure, server busbars, and the high-bandwidth interconnects inside AI rack systems. Freeport commands roughly 12% of global copper production and is essentially a leveraged bet on global electrification.
ticker_fcx.recent: Copper demand from AI data-center construction has become a notable demand driver alongside traditional grid and EV cable use, though Freeport's copper-to-AI revenue linkage remains indirect and diffuse. The company reported strong operational results through 2025, though it faces ongoing cost inflation at Grasberg. AI-related copper demand, while real, represents a relatively small share of total copper consumption today.

sources.title: Semiconductors in 2026: The AI-Driven Upswing Meets Structural Bottlenecks — Medium

ticker_4063-t.name: Shin-Etsu Chemical Co., Ltd.
ticker_4063-t.blurb: Shin-Etsu Chemical is a Japanese diversified chemical conglomerate and one of the world's largest chemical companies by market capitalization. Its two dominant businesses are polyvinyl chloride (PVC), where it holds the global number-one position, and semiconductor silicon wafers, where it is likewise the world's leading supplier. The company also produces silicones, rare-earth magnets, and cellulose derivatives, serving industries ranging from construction and electronics to automotive and pharmaceuticals. Its consistent profitability and conservative balance sheet have made it a benchmark blue-chip within Japanese equities.

ticker_3436-t.name: Sumco Corporation
ticker_3436-t.blurb: Sumco Corporation is a Japanese semiconductor materials company that manufactures and sells silicon wafers used in chip fabrication. Its product portfolio spans polished, annealed, epitaxial, junction-isolated, silicon-on-insulator, and reclaimed polished wafers, as well as monocrystalline ingots. The company operates globally across Japan, the United States, China, Taiwan, South Korea, and Europe. Formerly known as Sumitomo Mitsubishi Silicon Corp., it rebranded as Sumco in August 2005 and is headquartered in Minato, Tokyo.
ticker_3436-t.recent: Sumco reported earnings on May 12, 2026, with trailing twelve-month net income remaining negative at -¥23.27B and EPS of -¥66.53, reflecting continued softness in the silicon wafer market. Morningstar noted that forward guidance remains weak but raised its fair value estimate to ¥1,440, signaling an upbeat longer-term outlook. The stock has surged roughly 241% over the past year, trading around ¥3,427 on May 14, 2026, with a 52-week range of ¥937–¥3,859.

ticker_3037-tw.name: Unimicron Technology Corp.
ticker_3037-tw.blurb: Unimicron Technology Corp. is a Taiwan-based manufacturer of printed circuit boards (PCBs) and IC substrates, serving the semiconductor and electronics industries. The company is a key supplier for advanced packaging solutions, including substrates for high-performance computing and AI chips. It holds a strong market position as one of the world's largest IC substrate producers, competing with companies like Ibiden and Shinko Electric Industries.
ticker_3037-tw.recent: In the past 30 days, Unimicron's stock has been influenced by broader semiconductor demand trends and AI-related optimism. The company reported steady revenue growth, supported by robust demand for ABF substrates used in AI and data center applications. Analysts have highlighted its potential to benefit from increased chip packaging complexity, though near-term price action has been mixed amid global economic uncertainties.

ticker_asml.name: ASML Holding N.V.
ticker_asml.blurb: ASML is a Dutch semiconductor equipment company and the sole manufacturer of EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography machines — the tools required to print the finest circuit features on leading-edge chips at 5nm and below. Every AI accelerator, high-bandwidth memory chip, and advanced logic die manufactured at TSMC, Samsung, or Intel passes through ASML optics. The company's monopoly position emerged after decades of public-private R&D investment in partnership with European governments and chipmakers.
ticker_asml.recent: ASML reported €32.7 billion in total net sales for full-year 2025, up roughly 16% year-on-year, with net income of €9.6 billion and a gross margin of 52.8%. Year-end backlog stood at €38.8 billion. Q4 2025 saw record total net sales of €9.7 billion, including revenue recognized for the first High-NA EUV systems — the next-generation machines required for 2nm nodes and below. TSMC accounts for an estimated 40% of EUV tool deliveries. ASML guides to €34–39 billion for 2026 and €44–60 billion by 2030 as High-NA adoption widens. In December 2025 Huawei and Chinese startup SiCarrier confirmed a functional EUV light source using an alternative plasma architecture, but analysts place production-ready Chinese competition no earlier than 2028–2030.
